extracted.intended_audience: authors of systematic reviews and meta-analyses (and journal editors/peer reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how to report the methods, results, synthesis, and interpretation of systematic reviews and meta-analyses to ensure clarity, transparency, and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of summary data by outcome type
rubrics_metrics.description: For each study, provide summary data for each intervention group: for binary outcomes give frequencies with and without the event (or proportions, e.g., 12/45); for continuous outcomes give mean, standard deviation, and sample size for each group; for time-to-event data report the log hazard ratio and its standard error (or confidence interval).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the required summary data to allow calculation and pooling of effects. Provide group-specific numerical summary data (not only percentages) whenever possible to enable meta-analysis and re-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imputation and reporting of estimated/missing data
rubrics_metrics.description: When essential data are missing from included study reports and cannot be calculated, reviewers may need to impute values (e.g., imputing a standard deviation using typical SDs from other trials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly indicate which results were not reported directly and had to be estimated or imputed (see Item 14). Note inclusion of unpublished data. Justify imputation methods and, where relevant, report sensitivity analyses that assess the impact of imputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 21: Syntheses of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the main results of the review. If meta-analyses are done, include for each meta-analysis the effect estimate with a confidence interval and measures of consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show meta-analysis summaries with individual study results (e.g., forest plots). Make clear which included studies contributed to each meta-analysis. If meta-analysis was not performed, present qualitative syntheses systematically and explain why meta-analysis was not appropriate or possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forest plot and study-level presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting meta-analysis results, include forest plots showing effect estimates and confidence intervals for each study and, preferably, include numerical group-specific summary data, sample size, confidence intervals, and percentage weight for each study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forest plots should be accompanied by tables or inline numbers so readers can see the underlying data; include study weights and CIs. When too many outcomes exist, include the most important outcomes in the main report and provide others in a web appendix, justifying choices by the protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report syntheses for all pre-specified outcomes and note deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should report syntheses for all outcome measures they set out to investigate (those described in the protocol) and should tell readers if any planned main outcomes cannot be presented and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deviations from planned analyses must be reported; if many outcomes exist, justify which are included in the main report vs appendices. Failure to present planned outcomes (especially harms) risks selective reporting bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report measures of consistency/heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: For each meta-analysis provide a measure of the consistency (heterogeneity) of results across included studies (e.g., I2) and, where possible, a confidence interval for that measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report I2 and related statistics; where heterogeneity exists, explore and report possible sources and the impact on pooled estimates (see examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report harms and avoid selective omission
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide results for both benefits and harms for every outcome considered in the review whenever relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selective omission of harms biases a systematic review and reduces its value for decision making. If harms data are not reported in included studies, state this and consider implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 22: Risk of bias across studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Present results of any assessment of risk of bias across studies (e.g., publication bias, selective reporting across studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a funnel plot is used, specify the effect estimate and measure of precision plotted (typical x- and y-axes). Describe any statistical tests for funnel-plot asymmetry and report results of investigations into selective reporting across studies. State if pre-specified analyses for assessing bias across studies were not completed and why (e.g., too few studies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 23: Additional analyses (subgroup, sensitivity, meta-regression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give results of any additional analyses, such as sensitivity analyses, subgroup analyses, and meta-regression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify whether additional analyses were pre-specified. For subgroup comparisons report tests for interaction and provide effect estimates and confidence intervals within each subgroup. For meta-regression, report effect sizes and CIs (not only p-values). Specify the amount of data included in each additional analysis, and report all additional analyses conducted — not only statistically significant ones. Interpret exploratory analyses cautiously because multiple analyses can mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 24: Summary of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize the main findings including the strength of evidence for each main outcome and consider their relevance to key groups (e.g., health care providers, users, policy makers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a brief balanced summary of the nature and findings of the review. Discuss applicability of findings to different patients, settings, and target audiences. Where appropriate, present formal ratings of the overall body of evidence (e.g., GRADE) and tie summary recommendations to those assessments. Clarify trade-offs and how stakeholder values might affect decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 25: Limitations (outcome, study, and review level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss limitations at the outcome level (e.g., risk of bias), at the study level (e.g., imprecision, missing data), and at the review level (e.g., incomplete retrieval of research, reporting bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address validity (risk of bias) and reporting (informativeness) of included studies and generalizability/applicability. Discuss limitations of the review process such as language restrictions, difficulties in study selection or appraisal, poor reporting in primary studies, reliance on imputation, and how these limitations affect interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 26: Conclusions and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a general interpretation of the results in the context of other evidence, and implications for future research and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate review results to other relevant evidence and systematic reviews. State when conclusions cannot be drawn because of too few reliable studies or too much uncertainty. Make explicit recommendations for future research (e.g., interventions, participant types, outcome measures) when appropriate, and consider policy/practice implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 27: Funding and role of funders
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe sources of funding or other support for the systematic review and the role of funders in the conduct and reporting of the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report any funding or services provided (e.g., librarian support, access to databases), whether the funder had any role in study design, data collection/analysis/interpretation, writing, or decision to submit, and any real or perceived conflicts of interest. Transparency is essential because funding source can influence conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting requirements for other types of systematic reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-randomized intervention reviews and other review types (e.g., individual patient data meta-analyses, realist reviews, meta-narrative reviews, network/meta-network analyses), reporting demands may differ and extra information about methods may be needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure methods are reported with adequate clarity and transparency so readers can judge the evidence and replicate or update research. Individual patient data reviews require additional methodological detail; network meta-analyses should describe use of direct and indirect comparisons and how comparisons among interventions not directly compared were made. Tailor reporting to the review type while preserving transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRISMA scope: reporting guidance not a quality assessment tool
rubrics_metrics.description: The PRISMA Statement aims to improve clarity and transparency of reporting of systematic reviews; it is not intended to be a quality assessment tool and should not be used as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use adherence to PRISMA as a substitute for formal quality or risk-of-bias assessment of the review's methods or included studies.
